background.definition: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a small blue cell tumor and is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents. This malignancy consists of cells that resemble primitive muscle.

list.listitem: 4.6 per million among children 0 to 14 years old
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children; approximately 50% of soft tissue tumors in children are rhabdomyosarcomas.
It rarely affects adults.
Unknown/sporadic
Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from immature muscle cells/mesenchymal cells.
TP53 mutation is found in half of patients.
The alveolar form is associated with PAX3-FKHR gene fusion or, alternatively, PAX7-FKHR fusion.
Histologic subtypes include embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma, pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma.
Fusion-negative rhabdomyosarcomas typically display loss of heterozygosity at 11p15 and gains on chromosome 8
Fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcomas have translocations between the FOXO1 gene on chromosome 13 and either the PAX3 gene on chromosome 2 or the PAX7 gene on chromosome 1.

list.listitem: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and results of imaging studies. C
Radiographs are the initial imaging; they should guide the selection of subsequent studies (CT without contrast or MRI). C
Biopsy is necessary to confirm diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Less persistent, history of bleeding or trauma

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: Prognostic groups from the Children's Oncology Group are shown below: Group I: Localized disease, completely resected; Group II: Total gross resection, with evidence of regional spread; Group III: Biopsy only or incomplete resection with gross residual disease; Group IV: Distant metastatic disease.

list.listitem: Symptoms are related to soft tissue mass growth in a variety of locations: head and neck, genitourinary, extremities, abdominal, thoracic, and paraspinal. Superficial tumors may be palpable.
Orbital lesions often cause proptosis, while paranasal involvement may cause respiratory difficulty.
Obstructive urinary or bowel symptoms may occur by mass effect.
Pain can be present or absent. Neurologic signs can occur with CNS invasion.

Obtain plain radiographs to guide subsequent selection of imaging. If radiographs are negative, order MRI without contrast. If radiographs are abnormal, order CT without contrast to rule out myositis ossificans, followed by MRI.
Biopsy is crucial for diagnosis; immunohistochemistry (including MyoD and myogenin), FISH, and PCR can identify known genetic causes.

European guidelines (2021) recommend MRI both at diagnosis and follow-up to evaluate the primary tumour, including evaluation of neurovascular structures and lymphadenopathy. Chest CT plus [F-18]2-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose PET/CT or PET/MRI are also recommended to evaluate patients for loco-regional and distant metastases.

European guidelines recommend the following studies for staging: 1) CXR, 2) CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, 3) MRI of base of skull and brain, 4) regional lymph node evaluation with CT or MRI with PET scan or biopsy as needed, 5) bilateral bone marrow aspirates and bone scan for selected patients.
Anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, pancytopenia, and/or elevated liver function tests can be present with metastatic disease.
Hematuria on urinalysis may indicate genitourinary disease.
Order creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, and ECG prior to initiating chemotherapy.
Consider lumbar puncture with cytology to rule out parameningeal disease.
Patient presents with signs and symptoms of soft tissue mass; diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy.

Obtain plain radiographs to guide subsequent selection of imaging. MRI without contrast is recommended if radiographs are negative; CT without contrast is recommended to rule out myositis ossificans, followed by MRI, if radiographs are positive.
Obtain additional studies to determine the extent of involvement (ie, additional imaging, liver function test, bone marrow biopsy).
Treatment is surgery and chemotherapy initiated with or without radiation, and follow-up for recurrence.

Long term follow-up of survivors of cancer presenting in children and young adults should be structured to enable recording of late effects as well as recurrence. A recent population based analysis of long term mortality after sarcoma in young adults demonstrated significant increased risk of death from second malignancies and other morbidities.
First-line treatments include surgical excision and chemotherapy with or without radiation. B

A randomized trial found equivalent survival for: (1) vincristine, dactinomycin, and cyclophosphamide; (2) vincristine, dactinomycin, and ifosfamide; or (3) vincristine, ifosfamide, and etoposide, with surgery and with or without radiation for treatment of local or regional rhabdomyosarcoma. B
Patients with metastatic disease may benefit from the addition of ifosamide and etoposide to vincristine, dactinomycin, cyclophosphamide, surgery, and radiation. B
Treatment is guided by three-step staging (local tumor group, stage, and risk group). First-line therapy includes surgical excision and chemotherapy with or without radiation.
National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines recommend treating pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma like a soft tissue sarcoma.

Complete resection with a surrounding margin of normal tissue is ideal but may be site dependent (ie, orbit, genitourinary). Negative microscopic margins are preferred. Sentinel lymph node sampling is performed at the time of tumor excision.
Chemotherapy is recommended for all patients with rhabdomyosarcoma. The Children's Oncology Group protocol recommends the combination of vincristine, dactinomycin, and cyclophosphadmide.

A randomized trial of 883 patients with non-metastatic disease found equivalent survival for: (1) vincristine, dactinomycin, and cyclophosphamide; (2) vincristine, dactinomycin, and ifosfamide; or (3) vincristine, ifosfamide, and etoposide, with surgery and with or without radiation for treatment of local or regional rhabdomyosarcoma.
Radiation is recommended for patients with residual unresected tumor and patients with alveolar histology. It is generally started about 6 to 12 weeks after the chemotherapy is initiated.
A case series of 20 patients found better outcomes with radiation plus vincristine and cyclophosphamide compared with radiation therapy alone.
Clinical trials are under way to evaluate stem cell rescue after high-dose chemotherapy.

Patients with metastatic disease at diagnosis have been treated with ifosfamide/etoposide, vincristine/melphalan, and irinotecan, but this group has a relatively poor prognosis despite treatment. A systematic review found only three clinical trials, none of them randomized, of high dose chemotherapy for stage 4 rhabdomyosarcoma. None of the studies found a survival benefit to high dose chemotherapy, but all were subject to bias.

A trial randomized 120 adults and children with relapsed or recurrent rhabdomyosarcoma to vincristine plus irinotecan with or without temozolomide. Overall survival was improved with the addition of temozolomide (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.35-0.84). Serious adverse events were more frequent with temozolomide (98% vs 78%).
Embryonal, botryoid: 95% 5-year survival. B
Embryonal, spindle cell: 88% 5-year survival. B
Embryonal, not otherwise specified (NOS): 66% 5-year survival. B
Alveolar: 53% 5-year survival. B
Anaplastic, undifferentiated: 45% 5-year survival. B
Follow-up for recurrence is based on risk stratification (ie, for low risk: 3- to 4-month intervals for 2 years, 4- to 6-month intervals for 2 years, and yearly for 5 to 10 years). B
Outcomes are worse for adults than children.
